newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: CARR WOULD HAVE LEGISLATED FOR FOX STUDIOS
New South Wales Premier Bob Carr says his Government would have been prepared to legislate, had the Land and Environment court ruled in favour of a challenge to the Fox Studio development.
Local residents last week lost their bid to stop the development of the Sydney Showground site for the studios.
Mr Carr says the Government was determined to get the Fox studios for Sydney because the project will provide jobs.
QUEENSLAND GRAINGROWERS WARN PM OVER MP'S REMARKS

The leader of the Queensland Graingrowers has accused the Prime Minister of risking export markets to Asia; Ian Macfarlane says John Howard's reluctance to challenge anti-immigration comments by independent MP Pauline Hanson has caused concern in Asian business markets.

Despite plans for a full inquiry into the pricing structures of the health insurance industry, the Federal Government has refused to rule out further rises in premiums; National Mutual was today given permission to increase some of its premiums by up to ten percent.
CUSTOMS SEIZE RECORD HAUL OF ECSTASY

Customs' officials at Brisbane's International Airport have seized an Australian record haul of ecstasy tablets. The designer drug, estimated to be worth more than one million dollars, was found inside shampoo bottles in a passenger's luggage on a British Airways flight from London via Bangkok.
PRIVATE HEALTH INSURANCE DEBATE
The Australian Private Hospitals Association has called on health funds to freeze premiums until after the Federal Inquiry into the Health Insurance Sector.
But the Federal Government says it won't rule out further increases, saying it can't reject legitimate requests by the funds.

Federal health minister Michael Wooldridge today defended the decision to allow some National Mutual Fund premium increases of up to ten percent saying disallowing it would have put fund members at risk.
The Hospital Association's Geoff Sam says the price hikes areconstraining moves to expand the private-health care market.
The inquiry into the Health Insurance Sector is due to report to the Government next February.
OPPOSITION REFUSE TO ACCEPT TREASURER DENIAL

The Federal Opposition has refused to accept the Treasurer's denial that he revealed details of a conversation with United States Federal Reserve Chairman, Allan Greenspan. Peter Costello was recorded by journalists yesterday saying Mr Greenspan had indicated he saw no threats to inflation.
"COOKIE MONSTER" NICKNAME FOR WORKER
A West Australian worker has been demoted and suffered a A$3,000 pay cut, all for literally putting his fingers in the cookie jar.
The Australian Pacific Air Conditioning employee took two chocolate-chip biscuits from the lunch room of his workplace in Redcliffe without permission.
The company alleges he stole the biscuits and took them back to his work area with the intention of consuming them, but says the matter is still being investigated and there'll be no further comment.
The Australian Manufacturing Workers Union has taken the case to the WA Industrial Relations Commission, but the matter remains unresolved.
Union Organiser, Mike Anderton, says the punishment does not fit the alleged crime, and the worker has had to suffer the stigma of being called "The Cookie Monster" by workmates.
SCIENTIST CALLS FOR PRACTICAL APPROACH TO CONSERVATION

An Adelaide scientist has told the 65th ANZAAS conference that spending animal conservation funding on species close to extinction was akin to putting someone with no chance of survival on life-support.
Adelaide University Associate Professor, Mike Tyler, says resources for the protection of wildlife should be devoted to recovery plans for species not yet endangered.
Professor Tyler says species close to extinction should be allowed to die out.
He says a lot of money is wasted on cases which are hopeless, and would be better spent saving species with a much better chance of survival.
CROWN SEEKS BAIL REJECTION FOR BONDI ACCUSED
A crown prosecutor has told a Sydney court that the man accused of killing a British tourist at Bondi a month ago has an attraction to violence and should not be released on bail.
Chris Maxwell QC says 22-year-old Aaron Lee Martin poses a substantial risk to the community.
Mr Martin's solicitor Leigh Johnson says her client will be pleading NOT guilty to the murder of 28-year-old British tourist Brian Hagland.
Justice Vince Bruce has adjourned the bail hearing until tomorrow afternoon.
